## What I ran

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `npx tsc --noEmit` | clean, no output |
| `npm run lint` | 0 errors, 8 warnings — all pre-existing, in `ProfileClient.tsx`, `TravelGuideClient.tsx`, `pointsActivityTable.tsx`, `titlebar.tsx`, `travelGuideForm.tsx`; none in a changed file |
| `npm test` (full, twice) | 67 suites / 555 tests passed both times (17.9 s, 18.9 s). All 9 `*.database.test.ts` ran; `seatAssignmentCoverage.database.test.ts` passed both runs — the #155 flake did not appear |
| `npx playwright test e2e/booking.spec.ts e2e/multi-passenger.spec.ts` | 5 passed |
| `npx playwright test e2e/booking.spec.ts` (whole file) | 4 passed |
| `npx playwright test -g "round trip"` (isolated) | 1 passed |
| `npm run build` | exit 0, "Removed 1 environment files from standalone output." |
| `npx playwright test` (full, 1st) | 27 passed, **1 failed** — `e2e/travelguide.spec.ts` |
| `npx playwright test e2e/travelguide.spec.ts` (isolated) | passed |
| `npx playwright test` (full, 2nd) | 28 passed |
| New/rewritten Jest tests against the **pre-change** component | 8 failed / 24 passed — exactly the 6 new + 2 rewritten tests failed |

Environment: `travel-app-db-1` and `travel-app-mailpit-1` were already up and healthy (Docker; podman not installed). A `next dev` (v16.2.12, started 08:58) was already on port 3000 and Playwright reused it per `reuseExistingServer`; it served the changed component correctly (the new `review-leg` assertions passed against it).

Skipped, with reason: `prisma migrate deploy` / scratch-database work — the diff touches four files, none under `prisma/`, so there is no migration to apply.

## Anti-vacuity check (the thing most worth reporting)

I created a detached worktree at `HEAD` (pre-change component), copied in the new test file, and ran it. All eight touched tests fail there, each for the intended reason — not incidentally:

```
✕ reviews every leg of the itinerary, not just the last one opened
✕ shows each seat against the leg it is held on
✕ still names one leg and one seat on a one-way review
✕ does not bill a lone traveller in a breakdown of one row
✕ breaks the fare down once there is someone to compare against
✕ labels a middle leg by position rather than calling it a return
✕ books both legs with the seat chosen for each
✕ confirms a server-priced booking without collecting payment card data
```

The middle-leg one is the clearest proof the helper is load-bearing:

```
Expected element to have text content: Leg 2
Received: ReturningDetroit, USA → Seattle, USA · seat needed
```

The four rewritten assertions are **not** weaker than what they replaced. The two Jest rewrites are strictly stronger: `Class: ECONOMY | Seat: 11C` only proved a string existed somewhere, whereas `getByTestId('review-leg')` + `toHaveTextContent('Seat 11C')` proves it is *inside the leg card*, and `shows each seat against the leg it is held on` adds negative assertions (`departing).not.toHaveTextContent('12C')`) that nothing previously had.

## Findings

**1. Your suspicion about the round-trip e2e is correct — both seat names are `11A` (coverage gap, low)**

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/e2e/booking.spec.ts:326-330`. I confirmed it empirically rather than by reading: I polled the DB while the spec ran and watched the booking get written.

- The two flights the spec picks are id 10 `MA404` and id 22 `MA405`, with identical layouts (`firstClassRows 3, businessRows 3, premiumEconomyRows 4, economyRows 20, seatPattern ABC-DEF`) and **zero** occupied seats each, so `button[title^="Select Seat"].first()` is `11A` on both legs.
- Poller output for the isolated run: `bookingId=1247 ... seq1 f10 seats[11A] || seq2 f22 seats[11A]`, then two seconds later `seq2 f22 seats[11B]` — that second reading is the later "Change Seats" step, not the booking.
- It is also `11A`/`11A` in a whole-file run. I initially expected test 1 to leave `11A` occupied on flight 10, but test 1's journey cancels its booking (`seats[CANCELLED-e01daab4-…]` in the poll log), which frees the seat again.

So `toContainText('Seat 11A')` on leg 0 and leg 1 are the same literal. What those two lines still catch: only one leg card rendered (`toHaveCount(2)`), a leg card missing its seat, and the direction labels being wrong per index — i.e. they do catch #152. What they cannot catch is a swapped pairing.

Does it matter? Not much, because the pairing is pure component logic and the Jest test pins it with distinct seats plus negative assertions. Two cheap ways to make the e2e discriminate anyway: assert `reviewLegs.nth(0)).toContainText(outbound.flightNumber)` and `nth(1)` the inbound (`MA404` vs `MA405` are distinct and already in scope), or pick a non-first seat for the inbound so the names differ.

**2. No test anywhere pairs a *traveller* with their seat inside a leg card (coverage gap, moderate)**

This is the gap I would actually act on, and it is the one closest to the point of the change. Every multi-traveller assertion is `toContainText` against the whole leg element:

- `__tests__/components/BookingCheckoutWizard.test.tsx` "breaks the fare down…" — `expect(departing).toHaveTextContent('Seat 11A')` and `('Seat 11B')`
- `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/e2e/multi-passenger.spec.ts:128-133` — Alice, 11A, Bob, 11B all asserted on the same single `reviewLeg` element

A regression that rendered `passengers[0].seatNumbers[legIndex]` (or reversed the row order) for every row would leave the entire suite green. Scoping to the `<li>` — find the row containing `Alice Smith` and assert `11A` on that row — closes it in one line. Note the old multi-passenger assertions had the same weakness, so this is not something the change introduced, but the change is what makes it worth fixing.

**3. `legDirectionLabel` still has a second copy elsewhere (consistency, pre-existing)**

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx:598` keeps `{index === 0 ? 'Departing' : 'Returning'}` for the booking itinerary rows. The helper's docstring says "both callers read the assumption from here rather than each holding their own copy of it", which is true within `BookingCheckoutWizard` but not repo-wide: when #131 lands, the profile will label a middle leg "Returning" while checkout says "Leg 2". Out of scope for this slice — but the docstring currently overstates the fix, so either the comment or the third call site should move.

input.content:
Found while fixing #152, which introduced a `legDirectionLabel()` helper inside
`components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx` to stop the seat-step tabs and the review
summary each holding their own copy of the rule. A third copy lives elsewhere.

**Verification status:** confirmed by reading the source. The disagreement is latent
— it cannot be reached until #131 raises `MAX_ITINERARY_LEGS`.

## The copies

`components/ui/ProfileClient.tsx:598` labels booked itinerary legs inline:

```tsx
{index === 0 ? 'Departing' : 'Returning'}
```

`components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx` now derives the same label from a helper
that handles a middle leg:

```ts
function legDirectionLabel(legIndex: number, legCount: number): string {
    if (legIndex === 0) return 'Departing';
    if (legIndex === legCount - 1) return 'Returning';
    return `Leg ${legIndex + 1}`;
}
```

## Why it matters

`MAX_ITINERARY_LEGS` is 2 (`lib/validation.ts:16`), so today both render the same
two labels and nothing is wrong. Connecting itineraries (#131) raise that cap. At
that point a customer books a three-leg trip where checkout calls the middle leg
"Leg 2" and their profile calls the same leg "Returning" — two names for one flight,
in the two places they are most likely to compare.

This is the shape of duplication #143 warns about: the same rule written out at
several call sites, each rewritten independently later.

## Fix

Move `legDirectionLabel` somewhere both can import — `lib/bookingItinerary.ts`
already holds itinerary presentation helpers such as `seatLabel` and is the natural
home — and call it from `ProfileClient` too. Small and mechanical; worth doing
before #131 rather than as part of it.

`lib/bookingItinerary.ts` is also where the vocabulary for persisted seat states
lives (`Not assigned`, `Released`), so co-locating keeps the leg and seat wording
decisions in one place.

input.content:
Fixes the defect #143 recorded as the most-reported finding of the roadmap
investigation — raised independently by 8 of 12 areas, never reproduced until now.

## The defect

Step 3 of checkout read `flights[activeLegIndex]`, whichever leg the seat map was
last showing, so a round trip showed **one flight card** on the last screen before
payment. The return leg was not on it. Seats compounded it: a traveller's seats were
joined into `Seats: 11A, 12C` with nothing saying which seat belonged to which
flight.

The confirmation step was fixed for exactly this during the round-trip work and
carries the reasoning in a comment; review was the half that was missed.

## The fix

One card per leg in itinerary order, each carrying that leg's flight details and each
traveller's seat **on that leg**.

Moving seats into the leg cards left the fare rows repeating a name already given
once per leg — and for a lone traveller, a "breakdown" of one row identical to the
total directly beneath it. That case now states the cabin and stops.

## From the `ui-review` pass

It exercised one-way, round-trip, 2-, 3- and 9-passenger bookings at 390/768/1440,
plus the submitting state and a real concurrent seat conflict. Two blocking defects
in the new markup, both fixed:

- **A long name pushed the seat outside the card and the page into horizontal
  scroll** at 390px — measured, the seat landed 93px past the card edge, so the one
  traveller with a long name saw no seat at all. `lib/validation.ts` allows
  100-character names, so this was reachable input, not a contrived fixture.
- **A hyphenated name broke the name↔seat pairing**: the seat wrapped to two lines
  and ended up adjacent to the *next* traveller's name — the same class of confusion
  this change exists to remove.

Also applied: `role="list"` on both lists and an accessible name on the per-leg list
(WebKit strips list semantics from `list-style: none`), an "Itinerary" heading so
heading navigation no longer skips the legs, and a contrast lift on the direction
eyebrow, which was the dimmest text on the card despite being the discriminator that
matters.

It confirmed the fix reports the seat actually held rather than the seat clicked —
the group auto-allocator had reassigned one, and review followed the assignment.

## The e2e assertion that never could have caught this

`e2e/booking.spec.ts` asserted `text=Seats: 11A, 12C` on the review step and passed
throughout the defect's life: a pooled list reads the same whether or not the seats
are paired with the right legs. Both it and `e2e/multi-passenger.spec.ts` now assert
seat against traveller, row by row.

The verifier caught that both legs of that spec were picking `11A` — identical empty
layouts, `.first()` on each — which would have made the new assertions
near-tautologies. The inbound leg now takes a different seat so the check
discriminates.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, full Jest (555 passing, twice), the three changed
e2e specs, and `npm run build` — all clean. The verifier also ran the new tests
against the **pre-change** component in a detached worktree: all eight touched tests
fail there, each for its intended reason, so none of them pass vacuously.

## Filed rather than fixed here

- #158 — the boarding pass still says `GEMINI AIRWAYS`, and `productIdentity.test.ts`
  misses it because its regex is case-sensitive
- #159 — a seat-conflict rejection is invisible on phone, drops focus to `<body>`,
  and leaves the refused seat showing in success green
- #160 — `ProfileClient` keeps a third copy of the direction label and will disagree
  with checkout about a middle leg once #131 lands

Also noted the review step as a call site on #84, which owns timezone-aware
departure display — the leg cards show a date but no time.

#152 is fixed and merged as `a27af24`. Issue auto-closed, branch deleted.

## What the fix does

Checkout's review step now renders one card per leg in itinerary order, each carrying that leg's flight and each traveller's seat **on that leg**. Previously it read `flights[activeLegIndex]` — whichever leg the seat map was last showing — so a round trip showed one flight card on the last screen before payment, with seats pooled into `Seats: 11A, 12C` and nothing saying which was which.

Moving seats into the leg cards exposed a second problem: the fare rows then repeated a name already given once per leg, and a lone traveller got a "breakdown" of one row identical to the total beneath it. That case now states the cabin and stops.

## What the two review passes caught

`ui-review` exercised the rendered app across one-way, round-trip, and 2/3/9-passenger bookings at three viewports, and found **two blocking defects in my new markup**:

- A 100-character name — valid input per `lib/validation.ts` — pushed the seat 93px outside the card and the page into horizontal scroll. The one traveller with a long name saw no seat at all, which is precisely the information this change exists to surface.
- A hyphenated name made the seat wrap to two lines and land adjacent to the *next* traveller's name — the same confusion the change was meant to remove.

Both fixed, plus list semantics for WebKit, an accessible name on the per-leg list, an "Itinerary" heading, and a contrast lift on the direction eyebrow.

`verifier` ran the new tests against the **pre-change** component in a detached worktree: all eight touched tests fail there for their intended reasons, so none pass vacuously. It also caught that both legs of the round-trip e2e were picking seat `11A`, which would have made my new assertions near-tautologies.

## One thing worth knowing

The old e2e asserted `text=Seats: 11A, 12C` on the review step and **passed for the defect's entire life** — a pooled list reads identically whether or not seats are paired with the right legs. That's why 8 of 12 investigation areas could report this while the suite stayed green. Both specs now assert seat against traveller, row by row.

## Filed rather than absorbed

- **#158** — boarding pass still says `GEMINI AIRWAYS`; `productIdentity.test.ts` misses it because its regex is case-sensitive. Distinct from #140, which is about the drawn SVG.
- **#159** — seat-conflict rejection is invisible on phone, drops focus to `<body>`, and leaves the refused seat showing in success green.

content.text:
Here's the workflow as it now stands in AGENTS.md, unchanged except where noted.

## The eleven steps

1. **Inspect before changing anything** — repo, git state, instruction files; preserve unrelated work.
2. **Create a branch first** — never commit to `main`, branch from latest `main`.
3. **Choose a thin vertical slice** — smallest end-to-end slice that ships independently. **← new sentence here**
4. **TDD when testable** — failing test first, confirm it fails for the expected reason, smallest change, refactor only while green.
5. **Inspect the complete diff** — branch diff plus staged, unstaged, untracked.
6. **Run `ui-review`** — rendered app at phone/tablet/desktop, or explicitly record "not applicable".
7. **Run `verifier`** — builds, static checks, tests, coverage; rerun it if a finding causes a code change.
8. **Code review before every commit** — the `PreToolUse` hooks on push and `gh pr create`, plus `/code-review` for a full pass.
9. **Commit after approval** — Conventional Commits, ≤72-char subject.
10. **PR from the reviewed state** — ready-for-review by default, not draft.
11. **Merge only clean, passing PRs** — squash, then delete the branch.

## What changed

Step 3 gained one sentence: when work surfaces something outside the current slice, **don't widen the slice to absorb it** — file it and carry on.

Issue Tracking gained the substance:

- **File anything found but not fixed**, before moving on. A finding recorded only in a commit message, PR comment, or chat reply is a finding that gets lost. Search open issues first; comment rather than duplicate.
- The issue states **file and line, what was observed, why it matters**, and whether it was **verified against running code or only read in the source**. `roadmap` label only for phase work.
- **Filing is not a substitute for finishing.** If the finding makes the slice wrong or unsafe to ship, say so and stop instead of filing around it.

## How it actually behaved on #152

The rule fired six times in one slice, which is a fair sample of what to expect:

| Found | Where it came from | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| #155 flaky test | verifier | filed |
| #156 AGENTS.md drift | writing the rule itself | filed |
| #158 `GEMINI AIRWAYS` on the boarding pass | reading the file I was editing | filed |
| #159 seat-conflict error path | ui-review | filed |
| #160 third copy of the leg label | verifier | filed |
| Missing departure times | ui-review | **not** filed — already in #84's scope, commented there instead |

The last row is the one that matters most: the rule says search first and comment rather than duplicate, and that's the branch that keeps this from turning into issue spam. The itinerary-ordering finding from #143 also stayed unfiled, because I never verified it — filing an unsubstantiated issue is the failure mode the "verified or only read" line exists to prevent.

One friction point worth flagging: **step numbers are load-bearing**. `.claude/agents/ui-review.md` and `verifier.md` cite "step 6" and "step 7" in their frontmatter, and nothing tests that coupling — which is why the new rule went into step 3 rather than becoming a step 12. That's #156, still open.

Verify the change on branch `fix/redact-prisma-error-logs` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app, per AGENTS.md step 7. The change is uncommitted — use `git diff` plus the untracked file, not `git diff main...HEAD`.

## What changed and why

Issue #142: `lib/prisma.ts` enabled Prisma's `error` log level outside development. A Postgres error embeds the offending row in its `detail`, so a customer email address reached stdout in production — observed in this repo's own e2e output.

`lib/prisma.ts` now branches: development keeps stdout `['query','warn','error']` as before; every other environment constructs the client with `emit: 'event'` for `warn` and `error` and subscribes handlers that write `redactPrismaLogEvent(...)` instead.

`redactPrismaLogEvent` is a **whitelist**, newly exported: it returns `{ level, target, code, relation, constraint }` parsed out of the message with regexes, and drops everything else including the message text. That is a deliberate tradeoff — an operator gets SQLSTATE plus schema names but not the values behind a failure — and it fails closed on an unrecognised message (all three fields null, nothing logged from the text).

New test file `__tests__/security/prismaLogging.test.ts` covers redaction and delivery. `__tests__/lib/prisma.test.ts` was updated: it asserted `log` was an array of strings, which is no longer the shape, so its assertions now normalise through an `enabledLevels()` helper — the intent (which levels are on) is preserved, and its mock now returns `{ $on: jest.fn() }`.

## The part I most want challenged

Calling `client.$on(...)` at module load means importing `lib/prisma` now **throws** in a browser context, where it previously constructed inertly. That surfaced two test files that were declaring the wrong Jest environment and passing by accident — `__tests__/instrumentation.test.ts` and `__tests__/lib/env.test.ts` both test server-side concerns under jsdom, where `@prisma/client` resolves to the browser build. I added `/** @jest-environment node */` to both.

Please assess whether that import-time throw is safe in the real application, not just in tests:

- Does any client component, or anything reachable from one, transitively import `lib/prisma`? If a client bundle picks it up, this converts a silent no-op into a runtime error.
- Does `npm run build` still succeed, and does the standalone output behave? Check the build output for any client chunk containing Prisma.
- Is there a route or code path where `lib/prisma` is imported during a browser-side render?

If you judge the import-time subscription risky, say so plainly and propose the alternative (e.g. subscribing lazily on first use).

## Also worth checking

- Are the three regexes in `lib/prisma.ts` (`CODE`, `RELATION`, `CONSTRAINT`) correct against how Prisma actually formats messages? The test uses a real observed message, but I derived the escaping (`\\?"`) by reasoning about Rust's Debug output rather than by capturing a live event. If you can provoke a genuine constraint violation through the client and capture the real event payload, that would confirm or refute the escaping. Getting this wrong fails safe (fields come back null) but loses the diagnostics the change promises to keep.
- Does anything else construct a `PrismaClient` and log unredacted? `prisma/seed.ts` does `new PrismaClient()` — assess whether that matters.
- Is `redactPrismaLogEvent` genuinely unable to leak? Try to find an input where a row value ends up in `code`, `relation` or `constraint`.

## What to run

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, the full Jest suite, and `npm run build`. Postgres should be up already. Playwright is likely warranted since this changes a module every server request path imports — run at least `e2e/booking.spec.ts` and `e2e/auth-abuse.spec.ts` (the latter deliberately provokes the constraint violation that produced the original leak, so it is the best live check that logging still works and no longer leaks).

## F1 — `redactPrismaLogEvent` **does** leak row data — regression

The invariant the change claims ("assembled from named fields rather than filtered down from the message", "cannot carry a row") does not hold. Demonstrated against a live client, not by reasoning:

```
RAW: "\nInvalid `prisma.$executeRawUnsafe()` invocation:\n\n\nRaw query failed. Code: `23502`.
      Message: `Failing row contains (leak-1, u, relation \"LEAKED_USER_SECRET\" constraint \"LEAKED_TOKEN_9f3a\", m, null, f, ...).`"
RED: {"level":"error","target":"$executeRawUnsafe","code":null,"relation":"LEAKED_USER_SECRET","constraint":"LEAKED_TOKEN_9f3a"}
```

Mechanism: the three regexes run over the **whole** message, `Failing row contains (…)` / `detail: Some("…")` included. For NOT NULL (23502) and FK (23503) violations the message is *only* the failing row — no genuine `relation "…"` precedes it — so the first match is taken from row data. `[A-Za-z0-9_]+` accepts cuids, tokens, hashes, usernames.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `npx tsc --noEmit` | pass, exit 0 |

```
{ level: 'error', timestamp: 2026-08-05T17:59:46.608Z, target: 'verificationToken.create',
  code: 'P2002', relation: null, constraint: null, fields: [ 'identifier' ] }
```

`grep -c` for the address in the whole server log: **0**. That is the real server-side path, with `timestamp` present and `fields` populated — F2 and F9 confirmed live.

## Did the new tests pin F1 and F2?

Yes, mostly. Against the reconstructed previous version (old `CODE`, no `beforeRowData`, no `fields`):

- ✕ `refuses to read schema names out of the failing row itself` — fails with the exact leak: `"relation":"LEAKED_USER_SECRET","constraint":"LEAKED_TOKEN_9f3a"`. Pins F1.
- ✕ `reads the code the raw-query path spells differently` — `Expected "23514", Received null`. Pins F2.
- ✕ `names the columns of a unique-constraint failure` — pins F2.
- ✕ `says nothing rather than guessing` — pins the `fields` key only.
- ✓ `keeps no part of the row that caused the error` — **passes against the old code**. It is not pinning `beforeRowData`; the #142 payload happens to contain no trap words. It pins "the message is not passed through", which was already true.
- ✓ `keeps the schema names an operator needs` — passes against old code.

## Findings

### 1. `FOREIGN_KEY` never matches. P2003 is dead code. — regression against your F2 claim

Prisma 5.22.0 (confirmed: `@prisma/client` 5.22.0) does not emit the wording the regex expects. Live, from `prisma.review.create` with a missing FK:

```
Foreign key constraint violated: `Review_userId_fkey (index)`
```

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/lib/prisma.ts:67` expects `Foreign key constraint failed on the field:`. Side by side:

```
live msg   : {"code":null,"relation":null,"constraint":null,"fields":null}
regex wants: {"code":"P2003","relation":null,"constraint":"Review_userId_fkey","fields":null}
```

So a client-level FK violation still produces the all-null record F2 described, and the `?? (FOREIGN_KEY.test(safe) ? 'P2003' : null)` branch is unreachable in this Prisma version. Neither wording appears anywhere in `node_modules/@prisma/client/runtime/library.js` (both greps return 0) — the string comes from the Rust engine, so this can only be pinned against a live client, which nothing does.

### 2. Row data still reaches `relation` and `constraint`. — incomplete fix, latent

You asked me to find a message shape where the value precedes all four markers. Three, all live, all SQLSTATE class 22:

```
Raw query failed. Code: `22P02`. Message: `ERROR: invalid input syntax for type integer: "<value>"`
Raw query failed. Code: `22P02`. Message: `ERROR: invalid input value for enum "Role": "<value>"`
Raw query failed. Code: `22P02`. Message: `ERROR: invalid input syntax for type uuid: "<value>"`
```

Postgres puts the offending value in the *primary* message, not the detail. No `Failing row contains`, no `DETAIL:`, no `detail: Some(`, no `Key (`. With the value crafted as the patterns want:

```
{"code":"22P02","relation":"VICTIM_SECRET","constraint":"TOKEN_9f3a","fields":null}
```

Reachability today: none that I could find. All three raw-SQL sites bind safely — `lib/authRateLimit.ts` binds an HMAC hex to `text`, `lib/authTokens.ts:15` binds an integer `LIMIT`, `lib/flightLock.ts:6` binds a typed `number`. So this is latent, not exploitable. But the docstring at `lib/prisma.ts:37-38` claims *"Cutting first is what makes the extraction below a whitelist rather than a hopeful one"* — it is still hopeful. The next raw query that lets a user string reach a non-text column reopens F1.

Everything you *did* target is genuinely fixed. Probes A/B/C/D/E/H — raw CHECK, raw NOT NULL, raw UNIQUE, raw FK, `Prisma.sql` CHECK, and the `ConnectorError`/`detail: Some(` form — all with `relation "LEAKED_REL" constraint "LEAKED_CON"` planted in the row: **zero leaks**, and A/E still correctly returned `relation: "User", constraint: "User_email_canonical_check"` from before the cut.

### 3. `identifiers()` can emit a row value. — your specific question, answered no

It constrains the *character class*, not the provenance. Anything matching `^[A-Za-z0-9_]+$` passes, and plenty of this app's secrets are identifier-shaped:

```
cuid       : "fields":["cmscbchtn0006sizjhse9nkks"]
hex digest : "fields":["a3f19c2b8e7d4056a3f19c2b8e7d4056"]
non-ident  : "fields":null                              // ada@example.com, correctly dropped
```

A cuid, a `createAuthTokenDigest` sha256 hex, and a base32 TOTP secret all survive. What it *does* guarantee is that nothing containing `@ . - / + = ` or whitespace gets through — which covers email addresses, the actual #142 payload. Worth saying that in the comment instead of "a value that reached this far still cannot be written".

### 4. The `warn` path is entirely unexercised, and the F9 rationale is unverified. — coverage gap

I could not provoke a single `warn` event in 30 attempts, including a deliberate bad-credentials datasource override. That one produced an `error`, not a warn:

```
Authentication failed against database server at `localhost`, the provided
database credentials for `baduser` are not valid.
```

The only two `warn` emitters in `@prisma/client/runtime/library.js` are Accelerate/data-proxy paths (`Error while uploading schema: ...` and `Attempt ${n}/${m} failed for ${action}: ${message}`), neither reachable with a local library engine. I could not find the datasource-override-prints-the-URL behaviour you cite.

That said — **I do not think your conclusion is wrong**, just the supporting example. `Attempt n/m failed for X: ${i.message}` interpolates an arbitrary upstream message into a warn, and the credentials message above shows Prisma does put connection identity into log text. Redacting `warn` is right; the justification would be sturdier without the specific claim I could not reproduce. Note also that `console.warn` at `lib/prisma.ts:154` has no test and no observed live event — it is the one branch nothing has ever executed.

### 5. Redaction covers the log channel, not the thrown error. — scope note

`error.message` on the thrown `PrismaClientKnownRequestError` is byte-identical to the log event message, row data included. Anything that lets a Prisma error escape to Next's error handler prints the row on production stdout regardless of this fix. I found no such route (the register handler catches P2002 explicitly), so this is not a defect in the diff — but #142 is only closed for the log channel.

### 6. Playwright never exercises the server-side redaction. — confirmed, as you said

`playwright.config.ts:37` runs `npm run dev`, and I verified the dev server takes the `isDevelopment` branch (6 `prisma:query` lines on stdout). The redacted `23514` record that appeared during the run came from the *test* process — `e2e/auth-abuse.spec.ts:78` calls `prisma.user.create` directly under a non-development `NODE_ENV`. Useful incidentally: that is the exact #142 site, and it is now clean. The standalone boot was the only real coverage of the server path.

### 7. F4 confirmed clean

`PassengerInput` appears twice in `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx` — the import and one type annotation at line 549. `import type` is behaviourally a no-op. Found while fixing #142, which redacts the Prisma **log** channel. The same row
data is still on the thrown error, and that is a separate channel.

**Verification status:** confirmed by comparison against live events. No route
currently reaches it — this is a latent risk, not a live leak.

## What is still unredacted

`#142` moves warnings and errors onto Prisma's event emitter and writes a redacted
record instead of the raw message. That covers everything Prisma logs.

It does not cover the exception. `error.message` on a thrown
`PrismaClientKnownRequestError` is byte-identical to the log event message, row data
included:

```
detail: Some("Failing row contains (cmscbchtn0006sizjhse9nkks, Mixed Case,
Mixed-...@Example.com, null, null, not-used, USER, 0, null, null, null)")
```

Anything that lets a Prisma error escape to Next's default error handler prints that
on production stdout, and the redaction in `lib/prisma.ts` never sees it.

## Why it is not a live leak today

Every route checked handles its own Prisma failures — the register handler catches
P2002 explicitly, and server actions return `{ ok: false, error }` through
`lib/actionResult.ts` rather than throwing. No path was found where a raw Prisma
error reaches the framework's handler.

## Why it is still worth tracking

The protection is "every call site remembers to catch", which is the kind of
invariant that holds until one new route does not. A single unhandled
`prisma.*.create` in a route handler reproduces #142 exactly, on a channel that now
looks protected.

## Options

- A top-level error handler that maps `PrismaClientKnownRequestError` to a safe
  shape before anything renders or logs it, reusing `redactPrismaLogEvent`'s
  extraction so both channels agree on what is safe.
- A lint rule or test asserting no route handler awaits a `prisma.*` call outside a
  try/catch — narrower, and it would go stale.

The first is the one worth doing; it also gives customers a consistent error surface
rather than a Prisma string.

## Related

`prisma/seed.ts` catches and `console.error`s the whole error, which would print a
row. Assessed as not mattering: seed runs against fixture data in development and
CI, and a failing seed needs the full message to be debuggable.

input.content:
Found while fixing #142. That change stops customer data reaching stdout through
Prisma's log channel. It does not stop a caller writing *chosen* text into the
fields the redacted record does keep.

**Verification status:** reproduced against a live Prisma 5.22 client on three
separate channels, with real `$on('error')` events. Attempted and failed to escalate
it into third-party data disclosure.

## What happens

`redactPrismaLogEvent` in `lib/prisma.ts` extracts `relation` and `constraint` with

```ts
const RELATION = /relation \\?"([A-Za-z0-9_]+)\\?"/;
const CONSTRAINT = /constraint \\?"([A-Za-z0-9_]+)\\?"/;
```

`beforeRowData()` cuts the message at `Failing row contains`, `DETAIL:`,
`detail: Some(` and `Key (` first, which covers everywhere Postgres is known to put
row data. Class 22 errors do not use any of them — they quote the offending value in
the **primary** message:

```
Raw query failed. Code: `22P02`. Message: `ERROR: invalid input syntax for type
integer: "new row for relation "VICTIM" violates check constraint "TOKEN_9f3a""`

→ {"code":"22P02","relation":"VICTIM","constraint":"TOKEN_9f3a"}
```

Three reachable channels, all confirmed live:

1. **Parameterised `$queryRaw`** — the safe API. `` client.$queryRaw`SELECT CAST(${value} AS integer)` `` with a non-numeric value.
2. **Pure ORM, no raw SQL.** A type-mismatch validation error echoes the arguments object verbatim: `client.review.findMany({ where: { cityGuideId: <string> } })`.
3. `null value in column "x" of relation "..."` planted as a value.

## Severity: forgery, not disclosure

The extracted text has to be planted by whoever supplies the failing value, so this
does not expose another customer's data — the #142 concern. What it allows is an
attacker who can get a chosen string into a failing query writing chosen text into
the `relation` and `constraint` fields of production logs. That poisons the signal
operators read during an incident and can forge plausible-looking schema names.

Escalation to reading a *neighbouring* field's value was attempted and does not
work: the intervening `", ` characters fall outside `[A-Za-z0-9_]`, so the capture
group cannot run off the end of the planted string.

## What does not fix it

Anchoring the patterns to Postgres's sentence templates (`relation "x" violates`,
`violates check constraint "y"`) was tried and reverted. A caller who can plant
`relation "x"` can equally plant `new row for relation "x" violates` — lengthening
the phrase only lengthens the payload, and it costs the `42P01` / `42P07` / `42704`
schema-drift diagnostics, which are the ones worth most when a deploy meets an
unmigrated database.

## What would

Check the extracted name against the schema rather than against its shape — that is
provenance instead of pattern. `Prisma.dmmf.datamodel.models` gives the model names;
constraint names would need a list derived from the migrations or the schema. An
extracted name not on the list gets dropped, and a planted one never matches.

Worth confirming the `dmmf` import does not pull anything unwanted into the server
bundle before committing to it.

input.content:
Prisma's `error` log level is enabled outside development, and a Postgres error
embeds the row that caused it. A customer's email address was observed reaching
stdout in production through that path.

## The fix

Warnings and errors are handed to an event emitter rather than written by Prisma.
The handler writes a record built from named fields — `code`, `relation`,
`constraint`, `fields`, `target`, `timestamp` — and never the message itself.
Development keeps stdout logging unchanged, where the visibility is the point and
the data is seeded.

The message is cut at the first row-data marker (`Failing row contains`, `DETAIL:`,
`detail: Some(`, `Key (`) before any pattern reads it. That matters more than it
looks: a NOT NULL or foreign-key violation formats the *entire* message as the
failing row, and a row can contain the literal text a schema pattern is looking for.

Verified live on a standalone production server — three concurrent registrations of
the same address produced:

```
{ level: 'error', timestamp: …, target: 'verificationToken.create',
  code: 'P2002', relation: null, constraint: null, fields: [ 'identifier' ] }
```

`grep -c` for the address across the whole server log: **0**.

## Two things I got wrong, and what the evidence said

**The first redaction leaked.** The patterns ran over the whole message, so a
crafted NOT NULL violation yielded `relation: "LEAKED_USER_SECRET"` read straight
out of the failing row — and the test asserting that couldn't happen passed
vacuously, because its one payload had a genuine `relation "User"` earlier in the
string. `beforeRowData` and a test built on the actual leaking payload fix that.

**Then I over-corrected.** I anchored the patterns to Postgres's sentence templates
and claimed that made them a whitelist. It did not: a caller who can plant
`relation "x"` in their own input can equally plant `new row for relation "x"
violates`. Lengthening the phrase only lengthens the payload — demonstrated on three
live channels, including parameterised `$queryRaw` and pure ORM with no raw SQL
anywhere. Meanwhile it silently dropped the `42P01` / `42P07` / `42704` schema-drift
diagnostics, which are the ones worth most when a deploy meets an unmigrated
database.

So the anchoring is reverted, those three cases are pinned as fixtures captured from
a live client, and the comments now claim only what is demonstrated: `beforeRowData`
is a mitigation, not a boundary, and `identifiers()` filters shape rather than
provenance. What remains is a **forgery** risk, not disclosure — filed as #163 with
the real fix (check extracted names against the schema, not against their shape).

## Diagnostics that were missing and now work

Both confirmed against a live Prisma 5.22 client:

- Raw-query failures spell it `` Code: `23514` `` — capital C, backticks — which the
  original pattern never matched. The repo runs raw SQL in the auth rate-limit,
  token and flight-lock paths, so this was most of the errors an operator sees.
- `Unique constraint failed on the fields: (\`email\`)` carries no SQLSTATE,
  relation or constraint at all, and previously redacted to an entirely empty
  record. It now reports `P2002` plus the column list.
- Foreign-key violations: Prisma 5 says `Foreign key constraint violated:`, not
  `failed on the field:`. The regex was written for wording no live client emits.

## Blast radius worth knowing about

Subscribing at construction means importing `lib/prisma` now **throws** in a browser
context instead of sitting inert. That surfaced two suites testing server-side
concerns under jsdom, where `@prisma/client` resolves to the browser build —
`instrumentation.test.ts` and `lib/env.test.ts`. Both were passing only because
nothing had touched a client member at import time; both now declare
`/** @jest-environment node */`, which AGENTS.md's Gotchas already required.

`components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx` imported `PassengerInput` from a
non-server module as a value. SWC elided it, so client bundles were clean — but
`import type` makes that a guarantee rather than an optimisation. Confirmed: 0
references to `PrismaClient` across all client chunks.

`__tests__/lib/prisma.test.ts` asserted `log` was an array of strings. Its intent —
which levels are enabled — is preserved through an `enabledLevels()` helper that
reads either shape.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npx jest --runInBand` (569 passing), and
`npm run build` all clean. Three verifier passes, each re-provoking live Prisma
errors rather than reasoning about message formats; the second and third both found
real defects in the redaction, described above.

Note `npx jest` in parallel intermittently fails `seatAssignmentCoverage` — that is
#155, unrelated, and I added evidence there: it is a cross-file race, `--runInBand`
passes deterministically, and the orphan count is not always 1.

Playwright cannot exercise this path at all: its web server runs `npm run dev`, so
it takes the development branch. The standalone production boot above is the real
coverage.

## Filed rather than fixed here

- #163 — log fields can be forged with a planted schema name
- #162 — the same row data is still on the *thrown* error; #142 closes the log
  channel only, and no route currently leaks it

content.text:
Measured, and it settles the question decisively.

| Run | Wall clock |
|---|---|
| 9 database files, parallel | 8.97s |
| 9 database files, **serial** | 9.38s |
| 59 non-database files, parallel | 20.5s |

**Serialising the database tests costs 0.4 seconds.** They're I/O-bound on a single Postgres, so the parallelism across those 9 files was buying nothing — it was purely a source of races.

## Recommendation: split the run, don't weaken the assertion

Two phases in `npm test`: non-database files parallel, database files `--runInBand`. Total goes from ~21s to ~30s (the phases no longer interleave), which is the real cost — modest for eliminating the class.

## Why the obvious fix is the wrong one

Scoping the scan to rows the test created — the #150 pattern I cited in the issue — is wrong here, and the test says so at `__tests__/lib/seatAssignmentCoverage.database.test.ts:12`: *"against the whole table, not just rows this test creates (#137)"*.

The point of #137 was that removing the `Passenger.seatNumber` fallback is only safe if **pre-existing** data satisfies the invariant. Scope it to its own rows and it asserts that `bookFlight` writes assignments — which the second test in the same file already proves. You'd be deleting the coverage and keeping the file.

That's a correction to what I wrote on #155; the measurement changed my mind.

## Alternatives I rejected

**Per-worker database schemas** — the textbook fix, and it would make all 9 files immune permanently. But parallelism across them saves nothing (0.4s), so it's infrastructure for no gain.

**A timestamp cutoff** — scan only bookings older than the run start, since the invariant is about pre-existing data. Principled, but it needs a run-start stamp propagated into workers, and it fails silently if the cutoff excludes everything: on CI the seed runs moments before the tests, so a naive cutoff makes the whole assertion vacuous. Fixable with a "did it scan anything" guard, but it's cleverness where serialisation is free.

## One addition worth making either way

Add a guard that the scan examined a non-zero number of rows. The repo already uses this pattern — `productIdentity.test.ts` has an explicit *"scans the source it claims to scan"* test. Without it, a future change that empties the table turns this into a green test asserting nothing.

Want me to implement it? It's a small slice: two-phase test script, the non-vacuity guard, and a comment recording why the whole-table scan stays whole.

input.prompt:
Verify the change on branch `fix/serialize-database-tests` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app, per AGENTS.md step 7. Uncommitted — use `git diff`.

## What this fixes and what I found on the way

#155: `__tests__/lib/seatAssignmentCoverage.database.test.ts` asserted a whole-table orphan count and failed intermittently because another file's *intentional* fixture (a passenger deliberately left without a seat assignment) was counted while it was open.

Investigating turned up something worse. I added a "scans the rows it claims to scan" guard and **it failed**: the seed creates 1420 flights and 78 users but **zero** bookings, passengers, itinerary legs and seat assignments, so `Passenger JOIN ItineraryLeg` was empty. The orphan count has therefore been vacuous for its entire life — it was only ever non-empty when a concurrent file's fixture was present, which is precisely when it failed. It has never verified its invariant once.

So the change is three things:

1. **`jest.config.js`** now exports two projects, `unit` and `database`, split on `\.database\.test\.ts$`. `package.json` gains `test:unit` (parallel) and `test:database` (`--runInBand`), with `test` running both in sequence. CI runs `npm test`, so it is covered.
2. **The coverage test takes a booking in `beforeAll`**, moved out of the third test, so the global scan has a population to count. The scan stays global on purpose — that is what lets it catch a write path other than `bookFlight` leaving a leg unseated.
3. **A non-vacuity guard** asserting the join has at least 4 rows.

## What I want challenged

- **Is the split exhaustive and non-overlapping?** 59 + 9 = 68 suites, matching the previous single-project total, and 549 + 21 = 570 tests. Please confirm no file is silently excluded from both projects — that is the failure mode that would quietly delete coverage. Check the regex against every test file path, including any that contain `database` in a directory name rather than the filename.
- **Does serialisation actually fix the race?** I ran `npm test` three times clean, but the flake was intermittent at roughly 1 in 4 before. Try to provoke it: run the database project repeatedly, and consider whether anything could still overlap — `beforeAll`/`afterAll` hooks across files, an open handle, Prisma connection pooling, or a test that does not await its cleanup.
- **Is the guard load-bearing?** It should fail if `beforeAll` stops creating the booking. Verify that rather than trust it.
- **Did moving the booking into `beforeAll` weaken the third test?** It now asserts against a booking created in a hook rather than one it created itself.
- **Is the `beforeAll` cleanup still correct?** `afterAll` deletes by tracked ids. Confirm nothing leaks between runs — check for orphan `COV-*` flights or `coverage-*@example.com` users left in the database after a run, which would accumulate.
- **Does `next/jest` behave correctly nested inside `projects`?** That is the part of the config I am least sure of — transforms, `moduleNameMapper`, `setupFilesAfterEnv` and the jsdom environment all need to still apply in both projects. A silently broken transform could make tests pass for the wrong reason.

## Also

- Confirm the two-phase `npm test` still fails the build when a test fails (the `&&` must not swallow a non-zero exit), and that a failure in the unit phase does not silently skip the database phase in a way CI would misread as success.
- Timing: I measured the 9 database files at 9.0s parallel vs 9.4s serial, and the whole suite going from ~21s to ~30s. Sanity-check that.

`npm run build`, `npm run lint`, `npx tsc --noEmit` as usual. Playwright is almost certainly not warranted — say so if you agree.

Report anything still broken plainly.

content.text:
## What I ran

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `npx tsc --noEmit` | exit 0, no output |
| `npm run lint` | exit 0 — 0 errors, 8 warnings, all pre-existing in `components/ui/*` (diff touches no linted path) |
| `npm test` | exit 0, **6 consecutive clean runs** — `unit` 59 suites/549 tests, `database` 9 suites/21 tests |
| `npm run build` | exit 0, sanitize step ran ("Removed 1 environment files from standalone output") |
| Pre-change config, 68 files parallel | **3 runs: 2 pass, 1 FAIL** — the flake reproduced |
| `npx playwright test` | **not run** — see below, I agree it isn't warranted |

Plus targeted experiments: project-selection diff, resolved-config diff vs baseline, race provocation, guard mutation test, exit-code propagation both directions, `--detectOpenHandles`, Postgres connection polling, and before/after row counts.

## Answers to what you asked to be challenged

**The split is exhaustive and disjoint — verified empirically, not by arithmetic.** `--listTests` per project: unit 59, database 9, union 68. `comm` against `find __tests__ -type f` gives an empty diff in both directions, and an empty intersection between projects. The baseline (pre-change) config resolves to the same 68 files. Nothing is excluded from both, nothing is in both. No directory contains `database` in its name; the unit ignore regex is `$`-anchored so it can only match filenames anyway.

**`next/jest` nests correctly inside `projects`.** I dumped `--showConfig` for both projects and diffed every key against the resolved baseline config. The unit project differs in exactly two keys (`id`, `testPathIgnorePatterns`); the database project in exactly two (`id`, `testMatch`). `transform`, `transformIgnorePatterns`, `moduleNameMapper`, `setupFilesAfterEnv`, `testEnvironment`, `rootDir` are byte-identical. No silent transform breakage.

**Serialisation does fix the race, and I reproduced the race to prove it.** Under the pre-change single-project config with your new test file, run 3 of 3 failed:

```
● seat assignment coverage › leaves no passenger without an assignment on any leg of their booking
    Expected: 0
    Received: 2
    > 121 |         expect(Number(orphans[0].count)).toBe(0);
```

`Received: 2` matches the two orphan passengers `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/__tests__/lib/seatAssignments.database.test.ts` holds live (the `rival` passenger whose assignment insert is rejected, and the `createBooking` passenger in "refuses a seat whose flight disagrees with its leg"). Note your `beforeAll` move *widens* the window — the scan now runs after a full `bookFlight`, which is when the other file is mid-flight.

I could **not** provoke it with the new arrangement: `--selectProjects database` without `--runInBand` passed 6/6, and the two colliding files alone at `--maxWorkers=2` passed 18/18 (including 8 runs with a fresh `cacheDirectory` to defeat Jest's `shouldRunInBand` fast-test heuristic). The collision needs the CPU contention of the full 59-file parallel run to line up. So the flake is real but only reachable through the whole-suite parallel path the change removes.

`--runInBand` is doing real work, not being shadowed by Jest's heuristic: parallel 3.3–3.5 s vs in-band 5.9–6.2 s of Jest time. If Jest were already serialising, those would match.

**Nothing else can overlap.** All 9 database files `afterAll`-await their cleanup; the two phases are separate sequential Jest invocations; every non-`.database` test mocks `@/lib/prisma` (checked mechanically — zero unit tests import it unmocked). `--detectOpenHandles` on the database project reports none and Jest exits without a force-exit warning. Peak Postgres connections during an in-band run: **5** of `max_connections=100` — Prisma's pool is lazy, so the in-band process holding 9 clients is not near exhaustion.

**The guard is load-bearing — mutation-tested.** I dropped a temporary copy with an empty `beforeAll` into `__tests__/lib/` and ran it:

```
✕ scans the rows it claims to scan
    Expected: >= 4
    Received:    0
```

The temp file is deleted; `git status` is back to your three modified files. At-rest table counts confirm the premise: `Passenger 0, ItineraryLeg 0, Booking 0, SeatAssignment 0, Flight 1420, User 78`. Your vacuity diagnosis is correct.

**The third test is not weakened.** It asserts the same four assignments on a booking still produced by `bookFlight`, and if `beforeAll` throws, Jest fails all three tests rather than skipping them.

**Cleanup is correct, no leakage.** After the full campaign (6 `npm test` runs, 3 baseline runs including the failing one, ~30 targeted runs): 0 `COV-%` flights, 0 `coverage-%@example.com` users, 0 passengers/legs/bookings/assignments, flights back to 1420 and users to 78.

**Exit codes propagate in both directions.** With a temporary failing unit test: `npm test` exit **1**, and the database phase reported **0** suites — it genuinely does not run. With a temporary failing database test: unit phase green, database phase 1 failed, `npm test` exit **1**. CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:59` runs `npm test`) reads this correctly.

## Findings

**1. The timing claim in the config comment is wrong — coverage gap in the justification, not a defect.**

input.content:
`seatAssignmentCoverage` asserts a whole-table orphan count, so it counted the
passenger `seatAssignments` deliberately leaves unseated while asserting that seat
is refused. Roughly one full-suite run in four failed on another file's fixture.

## The fix

Jest now has two projects: `unit` runs in parallel, `database` runs `--runInBand`.
Nine files waiting on one shared Postgres gain nothing from running beside each
other, and serialising them leaves every assertion exactly as written.

The tempting fix — scoping the scan to rows the test created, the #150 pattern —
would have been wrong. The test says so at line 12: *"against the whole table, not
just rows this test creates (#137)"*. Scoped, it becomes a restatement of the test
below it in the same file.

## What the investigation turned up

I added a "scans the rows it claims to scan" guard, and **it failed**.

Seeding creates 1420 flights and 78 users but **zero** bookings, passengers,
itinerary legs and seat assignments. `Passenger JOIN ItineraryLeg` was empty, so the
orphan count has been counting nothing for its entire life. It was vacuous whenever
it passed and counting another file's rows whenever it failed — it has never once
verified its invariant.

Serialising alone would have made it reliably green and still worthless. So the
booking moves into `beforeAll` to give the scan a population, and the guard pins
that it has one. Checked: this was the only global count scan left in the suite;
#150 converted the other.

## Verification

The verifier reproduced the flake against the pre-change config (3 runs, 1 failed,
`Received: 2` matching the two orphan passengers the other file holds open), then
could not provoke it under the new arrangement across 6 full runs plus 18 targeted
ones. `npm test` ran clean 6 consecutive times.

It also confirmed mechanically:

- **The split is exhaustive and disjoint** — `--listTests` per project, `comm`'d
  against every file on disk: 59 + 9 = 68, empty diff both directions, empty
  intersection.
- **`next/jest` nests correctly in `projects`** — `--showConfig` diffed against the
  baseline: `transform`, `moduleNameMapper`, `setupFilesAfterEnv`, `testEnvironment`
  byte-identical, so nothing passes for the wrong reason.
- **The guard is load-bearing** — mutation-tested with an empty `beforeAll`, fails
  `Expected >= 4, Received 0`.
- **Exit codes propagate both ways**, so CI cannot read a failure as success.
- **No row leakage** across ~40 runs: flights back to 1420, users to 78, everything
  else zero.

## Corrections from that pass

My timing claim was wrong and is fixed in the comment: serialising those 9 files
costs about **3s**, not the 0.4s I first measured — my figure came from a cold-cache
run. The suite goes 21s → 31s. The decision stands; the evidence in the comment now
matches reality.

Three gaps it found, all closed here:

- The guard could itself pass on leftover rows from any source. Now scoped to the
  booking `beforeAll` created, expecting exactly 4.
- A `.database.test.tsx` would have landed in the parallel project silently,
  reintroducing #155 with no signal. Both patterns now cover `[jt]sx?`.
- My comment claimed another file's fixture "is never in the table at this moment".
  True of Jest files only — a dev server or a crashed test can still strand rows.
  Reworded: that is a true report about the database, and the fix is to clear the
  leftovers rather than narrow the scan.

## Documentation

AGENTS.md gains the two new scripts and a Gotcha, including that `npm test` no
longer forwards flags — pass them to `test:unit` or `test:database` directly.

## Filed rather than fixed

- #165 — two database test files never `$disconnect` (harmless at 5 of 100
  connections, but in-band execution is what makes it worth watching), and the haste
  collision warning printed on every run

## What shipped

Jest now runs two projects: `unit` in parallel, `database` with `--runInBand`. Nine files waiting on one shared Postgres gained nothing from running beside each other, and serialising them leaves every assertion exactly as written.

## The thing worth knowing

Adding the non-vacuity guard we discussed **failed immediately** — and that changed the fix.

The seed creates 1420 flights and 78 users but **zero** bookings, passengers, itinerary legs and seat assignments. `Passenger JOIN ItineraryLeg` was empty, so the orphan count has been counting nothing for its entire existence. It was vacuous whenever it passed and counting another file's fixture whenever it failed. **It has never once verified its invariant.**

Serialising alone — what I recommended — would have made it reliably green and still worthless. That's the failure mode the guard was there to catch, and it caught it on the first run. The booking now moves into `beforeAll` so the scan has a population, and the guard pins that it does.

I also checked this was the only global count scan left; #150 had already converted the other one.

## Corrections

My timing measurement was wrong. Serialising those 9 files costs about **3s**, not 0.4s — my original figure came from a cold-cache first run. The suite goes 21s → 31s. The decision holds, but the comment in the config now cites numbers that survive measurement.

The verifier also caught that my guard could pass on leftover rows from any source (now scoped to the specific booking, expecting exactly 4), that a `.database.test.tsx` would have silently landed in the parallel project reintroducing the flake with no signal, and that my comment claimed a stronger guarantee than serialisation provides — a dev server or crashed test can still strand rows, and that's a true report about the database rather than a flake.

It reproduced the original flake against the pre-change config, then couldn't provoke it across 6 full runs plus 18 targeted ones, and verified mechanically that the split is exhaustive and disjoint (59 + 9 = 68, empty diff both directions) and that `next/jest` nests correctly in `projects`.

## Also

AGENTS.md documents the two scripts and one gotcha: `npm test` no longer forwards flags, so pass them to `test:unit` or `test:database` directly.

Filed **#165** — two database test files never `$disconnect` (harmless at 5 of 100 connections, but in-band execution is what makes it worth watching) plus the haste collision warning on every run.

Four merged this session: #157, #161, #164, #166. Remaining in the cheap bucket: **#153** (`/flights` unbounded query), **#158** (`GEMINI AIRWAYS` on the boarding pass), **#160** (third leg-label copy). #153 is the one with real user impact.

input.prompt:
Review a UI change in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app on branch `fix/bound-flight-status-board` (uncommitted — use `git diff` plus the untracked `__tests__/app/flightsPage.test.ts`). This is AGENTS.md step 6, before the verifier.

## What changed

`/flights` — the "Live Flight Status" board. `app/flights/page.tsx` did `prisma.flight.findMany({ orderBy })` with no `where` and no `take`, so every row in the table went into the RSC payload on every request: **1420 rows, 404 KB**, spanning May 2026 to August 2027. Sorted ascending, the top of the board was therefore the oldest departure in the database. That is issue #153.

It now queries a window — departures from the last 24 hours through the next 7 days — with `take: 200` as a backstop. Measured result: **31 rows, 8.8 KB**.

Because the board no longer holds the whole timetable, `components/ui/FlightStatusBoard.tsx` gained optional `historyHours`/`horizonDays` props and renders a line stating what it covers, in two places: under the page heading, and appended to the "No flights found" empty state along with a pointer to the home page for booking further ahead.

## What I want reviewed

Exercise the rendered page, don't review from source.

1. **Does the board now read as correct and useful?** Before, the first rows were departures from months ago. Check what the top of the board shows now and whether the ordering makes sense for a status board.
2. **Is the coverage line doing its job?** The specific failure I am trying to prevent: someone searches for a flight departing three weeks out, gets "No flights found", and concludes their flight is cancelled or missing rather than out of range. Judge whether the copy actually prevents that read, and whether putting it in both the header and the empty state is right or redundant. Suggest better wording if you have it.
3. **The sparse case.** Roughly 31 rows land in the window today, but the seed is thin in places — check how the board looks if the window were nearly empty, and whether the empty state is reachable with no search term at all (i.e. genuinely zero flights in range). That state currently shows "No flights found / Try searching for a different destination…", which would be wrong wording when the user has not searched for anything.
4. **Responsive behaviour** at phone, tablet and desktop. The table already has `overflow-x: auto`; confirm the new copy does not break the header layout at narrow widths, and that the table still scrolls inside its container rather than the page scrolling sideways.
5. **Accessibility**: heading order, contrast of the new coverage line (`rgba(255,255,255,0.45)` on the page background — I expect this to be marginal, please measure), and whether the empty state is announced when a search empties the table.
6. Anything else actionable in the changed page.

The subtitle claims "Real-time departures, arrivals, and schedule status updates" — there is no live data source, and the board shows no arrivals. That is issue #84 (P4.2), which owns replacing the unqualified real-time claim. Please don't file it as new; do tell me if the new coverage line sitting directly beneath that claim makes the contradiction worse.

Departure times render with `toLocaleDateString`/`toLocaleTimeString` in the viewer's browser timezone — also #84.

- `docker compose up -d db mailpit` if Postgres is not up (podman is the documented fallback); it likely is.

- Capture screenshots at each viewport.

Report every actionable finding. Do not fix anything.

content.text:
I read the diff, exercised `/flights` in a real browser at three viewports, and measured the things you asked me to measure. Findings below, most severe first.

## What I verified working

- **Page never scrolls sideways.** `document.scrollWidth === clientWidth` at 390, 768 and 1440. The table scroller is the only thing that overflows (phone: 682px content in a 356px container, `overflow-x: auto`). The new coverage line wraps to two lines at 390px and does not break the centred header.
- **No console errors or React warnings** during load, search, filter and clear at any viewport — only HMR/devtools noise.
- **Focus is visible and tab order is logical** (nav → search input → status select), and focus stays on the search input when the table swaps to the empty state.
- **Sparse render is fine** — a 3-row board (search "Rio") just shrinks; no collapsed layout.
- **"search from the home page" points at the right place.** `/book` 307s to sign-in; the home page has the unauthenticated "Find your trip" form. Correct destination.

## Blocking

**1. The empty-state copy tells the user to fix a search they never made — and with the seeded data this is what the status filter *always* does.**
`components/ui/FlightStatusBoard.tsx:204-213`. Seen at all three viewports; screenshot `shots/desktop-empty-filter.png`, `shots/phone-empty-search.png`.

Select "Delayed" with an empty search box and you get, verbatim:

> 🔍 No flights found
> Try searching for a different destination, origin, airline, or adjust the status filter.
> Showing departures from the last 24 hours and the next 7 days. To book a flight further ahead, search from the home page.

Nothing there is true or useful for what the user did. They filtered by status; they are told to change a search term and to go book a flight.

This is not a corner case after your change. The whole table has exactly one DELAYED (MA202, 2026-06-10) and one CANCELLED (MA303, 2026-07-05) row, and **both now fall outside the window**. So on today's seed, "Delayed" and "Cancelled" are guaranteed dead options — two of the four choices in the status dropdown lead straight to this wrong copy. Before the change they returned a row.

The empty state needs to branch on cause, not render one string for three different situations:
- `flights.length === 0` (window genuinely empty, no user input) — must not say "try searching".
- query set, no match — name the query, and explain the window as the *reason*.
- status filter only — say no flights in this window have that status.

**2. `take: 200` can make the coverage line say something false.**
`app/flights/page.tsx:31-45` feeds `HORIZON_DAYS` to the board unconditionally, so the board asserts "the next 7 days" even on a request where the cap truncated the far end. The comment at line 27-32 acknowledges the cap drops the furthest-away rows; the copy does not. A user searching for a day-6 flight would then get "No flights found" alongside a sentence promising day 7 is covered — the exact failure mode you set out to prevent, just moved. The page knows: `flights.length === MAX_ROWS` means the window was truncated, and either the copy or the last row's date should reflect that.
I could not exercise this — the seed puts 31 rows in the window, nowhere near 200. It is reasoning from the code path, not an observation.

**3. The coverage line fails WCAG AA contrast. Measured, as requested.**
`components/ui/FlightStatusBoard.tsx:88` — `rgba(255,255,255,0.45)` at `0.9rem` (14.4px computed), normal weight.

- Composited over the actual rendered background at that spot (`rgb(18,14,26)` — body `#0d0c14` plus the `page-container` radial gradient, which *brightens* the background exactly under the header where this line sits): text resolves to ≈`rgb(125,122,129)`, **4.52:1 nominal**.
- Sampled from a 3x device-scale screenshot of the element itself, the brightest glyph pixel is `rgb(121,119,126)` → **4.31:1 actual**, because antialiased glyph edges never reach full alpha.

14.4px normal is not "large text" (needs 18.66px bold / 24px normal), so the threshold is 4.5:1. It sits on the line nominally and under it as rendered. For comparison I measured the subtitle above it at 7.19:1 and the empty-state text (which inherits `rgba(255,255,255,0.5)`) at 5.43:1.

The design problem is worse than the number: this is the single sentence that has to be read to avoid "my flight is cancelled", and it is styled as the least important text on the page — smaller and dimmer than the subtitle it is correcting. `rgba(255,255,255,0.6)` measures 6.25:1 and would still read as secondary.

**4. The empty state is not announced.** There is no live region anywhere on the page (`[aria-live], [role=status], [role=alert]` → 0 matches; the `alert` in the aria snapshot is the Next dev overlay). A screen reader user types into the search box, the table is removed from the DOM, and nothing is spoken — focus stays in the input, so they get silence and no way to know the result count changed, let alone that the board only covers a week. `role="status"` on the results container is the minimum here, and it matters more after this change because the range is now the most common reason for zero results.

Related, same block: "🔍 No flights found" is a `<div>` at 1.5rem (`FlightStatusBoard.tsx:206`), not a heading. It looks like one and is not reachable by heading navigation. Page heading order itself is clean — one `h1`, no skipped levels.

## Significant

**5. The top of the board still leads with flights that have already left, all badged "On Time".**
Screenshot `shots/desktop-default.png`, `shots/tablet-default.png`.

Browser clock was 2026-08-05 14:37 America/Los_Angeles. The first four rows are 01:00 AM, 02:30 AM, 10:45 AM, 11:00 AM — departed hours ago. The fifth, 03:00 PM, was 23 minutes away. At 1440x900 the rows occupy y=464 through y=894, so **every row in the first screenful of a board called "Live Flight Status" is a departed or imminent flight**, each carrying a green "On Time" badge, with no "Departed" treatment and no marker of where *now* falls in the list.

You fixed the severe version of this (top row was 2026-05-15). The residual version is the deliberate 24-hour history combined with ascending order, and it still means the answer to "what is leaving next" is not the thing the user sees first. Either mark past departures distinctly, insert a now-divider, or scroll/anchor the board to the next departure. Worth deciding explicitly rather than inheriting.

**6. "search from the home page" is plain text, not a link.** `FlightStatusBoard.tsx:210`. It is the only actionable instruction in the empty state, and it makes the user go find the nav themselves. `next/link` to `/` (correct target, per the redirect check above).

## Copy verdict — your question 2 and 3

**Both placements are right; the verbatim repetition is not.** The header sentence and the empty-state sentence are byte-identical, so the second one reads as boilerplate the eye has already dismissed, and it lands underneath a competing instruction ("try searching for a different destination") that points the user the other way. The two placements have different jobs: the header sets expectation, the empty state diagnoses.

**Does it prevent the "my flight is cancelled" read?** Only partly. "Showing departures from the last 24 hours and the next 7 days." states a fact and leaves the user to derive the consequence. Someone who searched for a flight three weeks out and got nothing has to notice the dimmest line on the page, remember their own departure date, and do the subtraction. Two things would raise the hit rate a lot:

- **Absolute dates, not relative durations.** The user is holding a booking with a date on it. "5–12 Aug 2026" is comparable at a glance; "the next 7 days" is not.
- **State the consequence in the empty state, not the range.** Suggested:
  - Header: `This board covers departures from 5 Aug to 12 Aug 2026.`
  - Empty state (query set): `No flights on this board match "GA999". This board only covers departures from 5 Aug to 12 Aug 2026 — for a flight after that, search from the home page.`
  - Empty state (window empty, no input): `No departures scheduled between 5 Aug and 12 Aug 2026.` — and drop the "try searching" line entirely.
  - Empty state (status filter only): `No flights on this board are marked Delayed.`

**Genuinely-zero-with-no-search is reachable** — I hit the identical render through the Delayed filter (finding 1). I could not narrow the window constants to produce it via an empty query, because I have no editing tools; however `filteredFlights === flights` when the query is empty and the filter is ALL, so an empty `flights` array renders exactly the DOM I screenshotted. Your instinct is right: that wording is wrong for that state.

## Suggestions

**7. `historyHours && horizonDays` is a falsy-zero check.** `FlightStatusBoard.tsx:31`. Pass `historyHours={0}` for a future-only board and the coverage line silently vanishes from both the header *and* the empty state — the one place it is load-bearing. `!== undefined` is what is meant. Your test "says nothing about a window it was not told about" would pass for the wrong reason in that case.

**8. The `plural` helper only pluralises half the sentence.** `FlightStatusBoard.tsx:24-25` bakes `the last ` into its return value, so it cannot be used for the days half, which is inlined as a second ternary on line 32. Two different mechanisms for the same job in one string.

**9. The query has no `select`, so 35% of the payload you just measured is fields the board never renders.** Confirmed against the live dev-server query log: `SELECT ... firstClassRows, businessRows, premiumEconomyRows, economyRows, seatPattern`. Measured on today's window: 8779 bytes full vs 5679 bytes with the eight rendered fields selected. Since payload size is the entire point of #153, this is the obvious remaining half of the fix.

## Pre-existing, not introduced here, but in the journey

**10. On a 390px phone the status board does not show status.** Measured column offsets inside the 356px scroller: Flight 0–110, From 110–231, To 231–352 visible; **Departure 352–476, Status 476–582, Price 582–682 entirely off-screen**, with no scroll affordance, shadow or hint. Screenshot `shots/phone-default.png`. Horizontal scroll inside a table is the hardest gesture to discover on touch, and the two columns that answer the page's question are the ones behind it. Not your change, but this change makes the board the authoritative live view, so it is worth a card.

**11. Table has no accessible name and no `scope` on any `th`** (`caption: false, ariaLabel: null, scopeAttrs: [null × 6]`). The search input and status select have no `<label>` — the input's name comes from its placeholder, and the `<select>` has **no accessible name at all** (aria snapshot: bare `combobox`).

## On issue #84

You asked whether the new line makes the contradiction worse. **Yes, measurably.** The three header lines now read in sequence:

> Live Flight Status
> Real-time departures, **arrivals**, and schedule status updates.
> Showing **departures** from the last 24 hours and the next 7 days.

The new line contradicts the word "arrivals" directly above it, and "the last 24 hours" undercuts "Real-time" — previously the false claim was merely unsupported, now it is refuted one line later by the page's own copy. Not a new issue; it does raise the priority of #84, and it argues for fixing the subtitle in the same pass rather than after.

## What I could not exercise

- **The `take: 200` truncation path** — seed puts 31 rows in the window. Finding 2 is code-path reasoning, not an observation.
- **An empty window via an empty query** — no editing tools to narrow the constants. Reproduced the identical DOM through the status filter instead; see finding 1.
- **Loading and error states** — the page is `force-dynamic` with a single server-side `findMany` and no Suspense boundary, `loading.tsx` or `error.tsx` under `app/flights/`, so there is no loading or error UI to review. A Prisma failure renders the global error boundary, which this change does not touch.
- **Real assistive-tech output** — I inspected the accessibility tree and live regions programmatically, not with a screen reader.

Screenshots: `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-scottdensmore-Developer-scottdensmore-travel-app/94121201-47c3-4281-aeff-7838379a510d/scratchpad/shots/` — `{phone,tablet,desktop}-{default,full,empty-search,empty-filter,sparse}.png`, `focus-input.png`, `focus-select.png`, and the contrast probes `probe-coverage.png`, `probe-subtitle.png`, `probe-empty-*.png`.
